articles.title: Active Lubrication Brakes in Tabletop and Hand-Held Haptic Surgical Drilling Simulators
articles.content: Haptic user interfaces that provide both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback have strong potential to enhance a wide range of medical training simulations. Yet, designing such devices remains challenging due to constraints related to integration, workspace, cost, and the need for diverse feedback types. To address these issues, we investigated the applicability of a novel type of brake based on the active lubrication principle. This actuator is compact, low-cost, and able to deliver both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback. To demonstrate its advantages, we focused on maxillofacial drilling in surgical training. We designed, implemented and evaluated a one-degree-of-freedom drill mock-up embedded into a tabletop prototype able to render axial forces up to 4.5 N. To assess both the relevance of combined feedback and the suitability of this actuator for surgical simulation, we conducted two studies: one with fourteen non-surgeon participants and another with six maxillofacial surgeons. Results confirm the potential of this actuation approach for surgery simulators and highlighted the importance of combined kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback to improve realism, user preference, and task performance. Based on the surgeons’ feedback, we then proposed a redesigned brake, with an improved control method, implemented in a new hand-held version of a drill replica. Preliminary characterisation shows that the new prototype can render forces up to 5.5 N and produce higher vibration amplitudes than the initial design.

articles.title: Reconciling Reduced the Sense of Ownership and Agency Toward a Virtual Keypad With Enhanced Haptic Experience Using Visually Adjusted Self-Haptics for Key-Input Interaction
articles.content: Self-Haptics is a tactile feedback technique where users utilize their own body to generate tactile sensations. This method allows the body to act purely as a prop, making it useful for virtual objects and user interfaces not directly related to the body. However, any method for maintaining the sense of ownership (SoO) and agency (SoA) of the user’s body and interaction targets that aligns with the perceptual interaction by visual cues has not been established. To address this, we present the concept of “(Not My) Self-Haptics,” which aims to resolve these inconsistencies, leveraging vision’s dominance in sensory integration. In this study, through the user’s interaction with a virtual keypad (VPad) displayed at the position of the real hand (RHand), we clarified how the user’s experience changed, including SoO and SoA toward the VPad, and how the task performance was affected by the interaction with the VPad. The results show that displaying the VHand at a misaligned position with the RHand or hiding the VHand significantly reduces SoO and SoA toward the VPad. Conversely, obtaining tactile feedback through Self-Haptics during interaction with the VPad significantly decreases task performance and increases SoO toward the VPad displayed near the VHand. Despite these unintended effects, this visual modification also significantly enhances Autotelics, Involvement, and Realism based on the Haptic Experience Inventory compared to typical mid-air interaction without tactile feedback. These findings contribute to the understanding of the interaction between visual and tactile sensations in Self-Haptics and the feasibility and practicality of “(Not My) Self-Haptics”.

articles.title: VibGrasp: Spatiotemporal Vibration Based Multimodal Haptic Rendering With a Lightweight Exo-Glove for 3D Shape Perception
articles.content: Haptic feedback has been employed to enhance shape perception during grasp interactions, improving immersion and task performance in extended reality (XR). Although wearable devices offer precise multi-phalangeal haptic feedback, their bulkiness and complexity often hinder practicality. In addition, fingertip-based tactile feedback often limits users’ ability to perceive a continuous and sequential sensation across the finger surfaces during power grasp. We present VibGrasp, a haptic shape-rendering method and a supporting haptic glove that synchronizes spatiotemporal vibrotactile feedback across multiple phalanges with 1-DOF kinesthetic feedback. Using the funneling illusion and duration-modulated vibration patterns, our approach delivers sequential, continuous sensations along the finger to render various shapes. We also develop a lightweight exoskeleton glove with two dorsal-mounted vibration actuators designed to transmit feedback to the ventral surfaces without obstructing motion. Two perception studies demonstrated consistent shape associations and clear preferences for specific patterns. A VR user-experience study further showed that VibGrasp achieved higher ratings for realism, satisfaction, and harmony than prior approaches. These findings offer insights into improving immersive and efficient haptic shape rendering in XR.

articles.title: Propeller-Based Handheld Force-Feedback Device for Navigation
articles.content: This article presents an evaluation of CrazyJoystick, a propeller-based handheld force-feedback device, for spatial navigation tasks in real-world and virtual reality environments. Building upon prior work validating the device's on-demand aerial deployment and directional cue discriminability, we investigated whether propeller-based kinesthetic torque cues can support effective wayfinding during continuous locomotion. We developed navigation-specific algorithms that generate egocentric directional cues using hierarchical decision logic optimized for dynamic heading corrections. Two user studies (N = 12) compared CrazyJoystick with vibrotactile baselines. Study 1 evaluated multi-waypoint navigation through four path configurations in a real-world environment with visual occlusion; CrazyJoystick reduced completion time by 54.6% and path deviation by 25.8% relative to vibrotactile guidance. Study 2 assessed target localization in a VR treasure hunt with minimal lighting; CrazyJoystick enabled 43.2% faster completion and 79% higher walking speeds. Both studies revealed consistent workload reductions. These findings demonstrate that propeller-based kinesthetic feedback supports efficient navigation during sustained locomotion, establishing propeller-based torque directional cues as a viable alternative to vibrotactile encoding for dynamic wayfinding tasks.

articles.title: A Wearable Shoulder Skin-Deformation Device Generating Illusory Forces for Posture Correction
articles.content: The hanger reflex is a haptic illusion in which skin-shear deformation elicits a directional force sensation. This study presents a wearable haptic device that uses four pneumatic airbags to apply controlled skin shear to both shoulders for posture guidance. Although previous work has shown that shoulder skin shear can induce illusory forces, neither the magnitude of these forces nor their influence on upper-body posture has been quantitatively examined. In Experiment 1, we quantified perceived force using a psychophysical comparison between skin-shear stimulation and real traction forces. The device generated perceived forces of up to 4.4 N in the forward direction and 4.8 N in the backward direction, more than an order of magnitude larger than those reported for conventional illusion-based haptic methods. Perceived force increased systematically with air pressure and was well approximated by a linear model. In Experiment 2, we evaluated the effects of these stimuli on upper-body posture by measuring trunk pitch under varying initial postures, stimulation directions, and intensities. The device induced consistent posture adjustments, particularly in the backward direction, with significant effects of both initial posture and stimulus intensity. These results demonstrate that shoulder hanger-reflex stimulation provides strong, controllable force sensations and measurable posture modification, supporting its use in wearable posture-support and rehabilitation systems.

articles.title: Sensitivity at the Edges of the Finger Enables Mixed Reality Force Feedback
articles.content: We introduce a new paradigm for rendering high-force sensations by stimulating the edges of the fingerpad rather than the central contact surface. This non-blocking approach preserves natural finger use, enabling simultaneous physical and virtual interactions. To investigate its feasibility, we proposed a mechanotransduction mechanism and conducted biomechanical and psychophysical studies. Our results show that the fingerpad edges are nearly as sensitive as the center under low forces, become roughly 117% more sensitive under moderate forces, and maintain sensitivity at higher forces. The edges also exhibit increased stiffness and tolerate higher forces before discomfort. Furthermore, the left edge exhibited approximately 143% higher sensitivity than the right edge in the right hand. Using these insights, we built a compact wearable device that provides multi-DOF force feedback without blocking the fingerpad and demonstrated its use in VR/AR scenarios. These findings support edge-based stimulation as a viable approach for high-force, scalable haptic feedback in mixed reality and teleoperation systems.

articles.title: ThermalTexture: Temperature-Integrated Surface Rendering Using Thermal Referral Induced by Texture Slip-Feedback
articles.content: Thermal–vibration feedback has been reported to elicit the thermal referral phenomenon, offering new possibilities for enhancing user experience. Yet, little research has explored whether thermal referral occurs in the presence of texture-slip feedback. To address this, we developed a custom haptic device capable of delivering integrated thermal and slip feedback to the middle and distal phalanges of an index finger. We primarily estimated the thermal referral occurrence under passive and active touch conditions across two different perceptual experiments, while each further examined its impact on texture perceptions and user experiences (UX). In Perceptual Experiment 1 (passive), we observed the highest occurrence of thermal referral at 40 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ (0.86 on a 0–1 scale), and found that referral increased the median of perceived roughness from 43.5 to 60 on a 0—100 scale. In Perceptual Experiment 2 (active), the kinesthetic cues significantly enhanced thermal referral, with the occurrence probability at 24 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ increasing to 0.86 compared to 0.51 (0—1 scale) in the first study. In addition, high UX ratings demonstrated the applicability of our device to temperature-integrated virtual texture interactions. Our findings expand the scope of thermal referral and highlight the potential for enabling VR users to interact with virtual surfaces that provide temperature cues.

articles.title: Subtype-Selective Neuronal Vulnerability and Compensatory Neuroglial Remodeling in Human Cortical Dementia
articles.content: Whether the nodal vulnerability in dementia is solely represented by changes in cellular abundance or attrition of cellular transcriptomic landscape attribute to that transition in aging brain is yet to uncover with minutiae. To understand this complication, we have analyzed two snRNA-seq data specific to (I) dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC): A comprehensive study of cellular profiling among cognitively normal and pathological ageing and dementia (AD) brain, (II) occipital cortex (OC) in the context of Nasu-Hakola disease along with a tissue level bulk RNA-seq data corresponds to temporal cortex. We pinpoint cellular subpopulations their proportional changes within the nodal points and their transcriptomic profiling. In DLPFC we observed alteration of mitochondrial and synaptic maintenance program in the pathological manifestation of disease. In OC we noticed depleted upper layer CUX2 neuron, PVALB and SST neurons on the contrary an enrichment of RORB and LAMP5 neurons with compromised metabolic states in the disease context. Glial populations are marked by representation of fibrous astrocyte, neuronal-supporting subpopulations associated with extracellular matrix remodeling programs. Proportional increment of intermediate myelinating oligodendrocyte and a decrease in mature myelinating subpopulation highlighted a compromised myelin repair attempt. In temporal cortex at tissue level we observed transcriptomic landscape adopted a neuroglial phenotypes in dementia brain. Cell-Chat analysis demonstrated a shift in cellular coordination towards glial population from neuron in NHD brain. A single cell-based drug reprofiling approach identified efatutazone and balaglitazone as broad-spectrum candidates for major cell types in occipital cortex, whereas major actionable biological targets belong to CDK subtypes and proteasome subunits. Overall, our findings imply cellular persistence do not necessarily substantiate molecular preservation, also the coexistence of cellular vulnerability alongside selective remodeling features, present a cellular framework on how to cope up with degenerative changes.
articles.author: Roy, B., Roy, P. K.

articles.title: From sensation to action: distributed mesoscale dynamics in the primate brain
articles.content: Perceptual decisions engage distributed brain networks, yet how decision-related signals are organized across and within brain areas remains unclear. Mesoscale functional domains are established in visual cortex, but whether spatially distinct domains organize perceptual decisions across the brain is unknown. Here we used 7-T functional MRI at 1-mm isotropic resolution in two awake macaques performing a contrast-discrimination task to map brain-wide activity during sensation, decision formation and saccadic report. Voxel timecourses separated into three groups with distinct temporal profiles, associated with sensory, decision-related and action-related activity. Their spatial distributions formed a broad progression from visual cortex to parietal, prefrontal and motor regions, while revealing distinct response domains within these regions. Choice-related signals were distributed across sensory, associative, and motor systems before movement, including in visual cortex responses to physically identical stimuli that differed according to the animal's eventual choice. Moreover, within the intraparietal sulcus and other regions, mesoscale domains preferentially responsive to near-threshold conditions carried choice information under uncertainty, whereas domains responsive to high-contrast conditions carried choice information when evidence was strong. These findings reveal that perceptual decisions are organized across the brain through spatially differentiated mesoscale networks whose activity varies with task phase and sensory certainty. This spatial organization provides a framework for investigating how distributed neural signals support flexible choice.
articles.author: Shi, S., Chen, M., Quan, Z., Zhai, C., Qian, M., Tanigawa, H., Jia, K., Zhang, X., Pan, G., Roe, A. W.

articles.title: The Onset of Breathing at Birth Switches Off Regenerative Capacity
articles.content: Many mammalian tissues, including the central nervous system (CNS), lose regenerative capacity in adulthood, but when and how this transition is initiated remains unclear. By monitoring mTOR activity, an evolutionarily conserved readout of cellular growth and intrinsic regenerative potential, we found that mTOR signaling declines within minutes after birth in murine CNS neurons and in other organs such as the heart and skeletal muscles. Focusing on retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), we show that this abrupt decline is driven primarily by CO2 exhalation following the onset of breathing after birth. Using real-time in vivo imaging of RGCs during the earliest postnatal period, we further discover that breathing-induced CO2 exhalation rapidly causes intracellular alkalinization, activates an AMPK-family kinase, SNF-related kinase (SNRK), which in turn suppresses mTOR signaling. Importantly, this process remains reversible in adulthood: CO2 inhalation or Snrk deletion restores mTOR activity in RGCs and enables robust regeneration of their axons after injury. Similar CO2 inhalation-induced mTOR reactivation occurs across multiple cell types and organs, suggesting a general mechanism by which breathing-associated CO2/pH signaling shapes the regenerative capacity across life and pointing to a potential CO2-based strategy for promoting tissue regeneration.
articles.author: Song, X., Cai, X., Hegarty, S., Speri, D., Yasuda, M., Donahue, R., Stanicka, J., Yan, T., Mao, S., Yang, S., Chen, J., Zhu, J., Kiraly, J., Chien, C.-H., Kegeles, E., Feng, D., Stieger, K., Yang, Z., Zhang, Y., Yellen, G., Umemori, H., Williams, P., He, Z.

articles.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
articles.content: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.
articles.author: Gulati, D., Rao, M. B., Mundlamuri, R. C., Arimappamagan, A., Sadashiva, N., Sinha, S., Kenchaiah, R., Asranna, A., Viswanathan, L. G., Ray, S.

articles.title: An Engineering Explanation of Human Vertical Reaching: Optimal Trajectory Planning of Asymmetric Velocity Profiles in the Vertical Plane via a Softplus-Based Generalized Dynamic Jerk Cost Function.
articles.content: The results in this article demonstrate that the central nervous system CNS plans trajectories in the vertical plane by minimizing a Generalized Dynamic Jerk GJerk cost function, which we have proposed as an advancement of the traditional Minimum Jerk cost function. While the traditional Jerk cost function generates smooth trajectories by minimizing the third derivative of joint angle over time, it neglects real dynamic constraints most notably the effect of gravity. According to our engineering interpretation, the arm functions as a constrained manipulator where gravity acts as a non-linear, state-dependent bias; thus, the asymmetry in velocity profiles is not an anomaly but an optimal adaptation to the gravitational field. Consequently, it predicts mathematically symmetrical upward and downward movements, even in contexts where gravitational forces play a decisive role. The proposed GJerk cost function extends the classical framework by incorporating position-dependent dynamic coefficients into the cost function, thereby embedding gravitational effects directly within the planning process. As a result, the generated movements are not only smooth in a mathematical sense but also physically and mechanically consistent with the actual torque and energy demands imposed by the musculoskeletal system. The GJerk cost function reduces angular change in high-gravitational-torque regions because it makes the joint configuration with the highest gravitational torque more expensive within the cost function, prompting the planner to choose a slower and more conservative movement. This does not physically dissipate energy, but it acts as a behavioral damping mechanism, similar to how humans naturally slow down when approaching a high load or potentially dangerous configuration. In this way, the GJerk cost function reduces abrupt changes in joint kinetic energy and prevents sudden jumps in acceleration, ultimately producing a smoother and more stable trajectory that aligns with both biomechanical reality and observed human behavior. Within this framework, upward movements become inherently more costly than downward ones, penalizing configurations that require large torques to counteract gravity. This induces a biomechanically meaningful asymmetry, ensuring the resulting trajectories reflect the body's true mechanical constraints rather than mere geometric smoothness. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GJerk cost function provides a more realistic and physiologically grounded account of motor planning in the vertical plane, linking smoothness optimization with genuine dynamic requirements and offering a closer approximation to biological motor behavior
articles.author: Kabbani, M. B., Marouf, A.

articles.title: Raf-MEK-ERK signaling mediates FLT3-induced mechanical allodynia and reduced morphine analgesic efficacy in male rodents
articles.content: The cytokine FL and its receptor, Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), contribute to chronic pain and to the maladaptive effects of morphine but the intracellular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the contribution of the Raf-MEK-ERK pathway to FLT3dependent nociceptive signaling and to the modulation of morphine analgesia. Using HEK293T cells expressing human or mouse FLT3, primary dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, and rodent models, we examined ERK activation, TRPV1 sensitization, and behavioral responses following FLT3 activation by its ligand, FL. FL induced concentration-dependent ERK phosphorylation through FLT3, while pharmacological inhibition of FLT3, Raf, or MEK reduced this response. In primary DRG neurons, MEK inhibition attenuated FLinduced potentiation of capsaicin-evoked calcium responses, supporting a role for MEK-ERK signaling in TRPV1 sensitization. In vivo, intrathecal FL increased ERK phosphorylation in DRGs and induced mechanical hypersensitivity, both of which were reduced by Raf or MEK inhibition. In FLT3/MOR-expressing cells, morphine potentiated FL-induced ERK activation, an effect reduced by naloxone and abolished by FLT3 inhibition. In rats, MEK inhibition prevented the FL-induced reduction of morphine analgesia and subsequent mechanical hypersensitivity. Together, these findings identify Raf-MEK-ERK signaling as an important downstream pathway linking neuronal FLT3 activation to nociceptor sensitization and impaired morphine analgesic efficacy.
articles.author: Leyris, J.-P., Ajas, D., Bertin, J., Sar, C., Mallie, S., Cunha, T. M., Ango, F., Moha ou Maati, H., Mechaly, I., Valmier, J., Rivat, C.

articles.title: Autonomic neurons are intrinsically hyperexcitable in a Friedreich ataxia iPSC model
articles.content: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an inherited multisystem disorder caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene and consequent frataxin deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration and heart disease. Clinical studies have documented autonomic dysfunction in FRDA, including elevated resting heart rate, raised plasma catecholamines and a high burden of urinary, bowel and sexual symptoms. Consistent with this, autopsy studies show degeneration of the cardiac conduction system and its associated ganglia in FRDA. Whether these features are intrinsic to FRDA autonomic neurons has been untestable without a human cellular model. Here, a human model of FRDA autonomic neurons was established by differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from individuals with FRDA and from their CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. FRDA autonomic neurons expressed canonical autonomic lineage markers and retained reduced FXN mRNA and frataxin protein levels. Electrophysiological analysis revealed pronounced hyperexcitability, with an approximately five-fold increase in spike number, shortened interspike intervals, and longer bursts. FRDA autonomic neurons also exhibited increased cell death, elevated mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and a shift from networked to tubular mitochondrial morphology. Bulk RNA sequencing of all three isogenic pairs revealed loss of extracellular matrix programs and activation of stress response pathways. The top differentially expressed gene was MEG3, a maternally imprinted long noncoding RNA, which was consistently upregulated across all three isogenic pairs. MEG3 sits within the imprinted 14q32 DLK1-DIO3 locus, whose maternally expressed noncoding transcripts were co-ordinately de-repressed in FRDA autonomic neurons. Competitive gene-set testing of 43 imprinted genes across 20 domains showed this to be specific to 14q32: no other imprinted domain was co-ordinately altered. Together, these findings establish hyperexcitability of autonomic neurons as a cell autonomous consequence of frataxin deficiency, accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction. This provides a cellular basis for the increased sympathetic tone observed in clinical studies.
articles.author: (Max), S. L., Lees, J., Zhang, H., Li, L., Dottori, M., Pebay, A., Corben, L., Delatycki, M., Wilcox, S., Pullin, J., Choi, J., McCarthy, D., Napierala, J., Napierala, M.

articles.title: Simultaneous recordings link intracranial and scalp correlates of somatosensory awareness in humans
articles.content: The electrophysiological events underlying the conscious perception of touch in humans remain elusive. Scalp-EEG studies have identified a negative deflection peaking 120-200 ms after stimulus onset, known as the N140. This component, recently reinterpreted as the somatosensory awareness negativity (N140/SAN), has been proposed as a putative marker of tactile awareness, but its underlying neuronal dynamics are still unknown. Intracranial studies have shown that responses to median nerve stimulation include, after an initial phasic activation mainly localized to primary somatosensory cortices, a predominantly insulo-opercular tonic broadband high-frequency activity (BHA; 50-150 Hz) that has been linked to tactile awareness. Yet these scalp and intracranial signatures have never been directly linked. Using simultaneous high-density scalp EEG and intracranial EEG recordings, we show that the N140/SAN is the scalp manifestation of the insulo-opercular local field potential that follows the BHA response to stimulation. By bridging invasive and non-invasive recordings our results identify the neural origins of the N140/SAN and connect scalp and intracranial correlates of somatosensory awareness.
articles.author: Mikulan, E., Zauli, F. M., Russo, S., Mannini, F., Del Vecchio, M., Albertini, D., d'Orio, P., Nobili, L., Sartori, I., Massimini, M., Avanzini, P., Pigorini, A.

articles.title: Serotonin2A receptors in the medial prefrontal cortex do not drive DOI-induced head-twitch responses in rodents
articles.content: Background The head-twitch response (HTR) is a serotonin2A receptor (5-HT2AR) dependent behavioral correlate of serotonergic psychedelic action in rodent models. Although cortical 5-HT2ARs have been implicated in HTRs, the contribution of specific cortical circuits to this behavior remains poorly defined, with a few reports implicating the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in the generation of HTRs. Results The serotonergic psychedelic, 2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI), induced head-twitch responses (HTRs) in male and female rats and mice, with sex differences noted only in mice. DOI also increased ear-scratch responses (ESRs), and reduced digging and grooming behaviors only in mice. While the DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs were absent in 5-HT2AR knock-out (5-HT2AR KO) mice, reduced digging and grooming occurred in both wild-type and 5-HT2AR KO mice. We assessed the role of 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC in regulating DOI-induced HTRs using pharmacological and genetic approaches. Targeted DOI microinfusion into the mPFC did not induce HTRs in rats, in contrast to the robust increase in HTRs noted following systemic DOI administration. Local delivery of the selective 5-HT2AR antagonist, MDL100907, into the mPFC also had no effect on the systemic DOI-evoked increase in HTRs in rats. Experiments capitalizing on genetic strategies to perturb 5-HT2AR expression in the mPFC, indicated that viral restoration of 5-HT2AR expression in mPFC CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons was not sufficient to reinstate DOI-evoked HTRs or ESRs in 5-HT2AR KO mice. Further, conditional 5-HT2AR deletion in CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons in the mPFC did not alter systemic DOI-induced HTRs and ESRs in mice. Conclusions These findings indicate that the serotonergic psychedelic DOI induces species- and sex-specific behavioral effects in rodent models, with a robust 5-HT2AR dependence noted for DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs. Further, we show that 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC do not appear to contribute to the enhanced HTRs and ESRs elicited by DOI.
articles.author: Vuruputuri, R. M., Reghunath, V., Mukherjee, S., Bajre, G., Chaudhari, P. R., Gahrotra, V., Vaidya, V. A.

articles.title: Oligodendrocyte ER-phagy Restricts Excessive Myelination by Degrading Sphingolipid Synthases
articles.content: Myelination is critical for nervous system function. Numerous signaling pathways have been identified that promote myelin sheath growth, disruption of which can lead to hypomyelination, characterized by a reduction in myelin sheath thickness. However, the negative regulators of myelin sheath expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a cellular brake on central nervous system myelination that restricts myelin sheath thickness during brain development. This brake is mediated by a selective form of autophagy, known as endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-phagy, which degrades the ER and its resident sphingolipid synthases. ER-phagy is highly active in oligodendrocytes during myelin membrane expansion, and its impairment leads to ER accumulation, elevated sphingolipid production, and excessive myelin thickening. Genetic reduction of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis in the ER rescues the hypermyelination phenotype caused by ER-phagy disruption. In summary, our findings establish ER-phagy as a key regulator of sphingolipid metabolism and reveal a mechanistic link between ER homeostasis and myelin production by oligodendrocytes, providing insight into mechanisms underlying pathological hypermyelination.
articles.author: Zhang, T., Barbosa, D., Bhambri, A., Sun, L. O.
